name: 10 Usability Heuristics
tagline: Jakob Nielsen's 10 general principles for interaction design, first published in 1994
description:
Nielsen Norman Group publishes Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics as a free article. The page calls them broad rules of thumb, not specific usability guidelines. The byline is Jakob Nielsen, dated April 24, 1994, and marked last reviewed on January 30, 2024.

The article names ten principles: visibility of system status, match between the system and the real world, user control and freedom, consistency and standards, error prevention, recognition rather than recall, flexibility and efficiency of use, aesthetic and minimalist design, help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors, and help and documentation. It credits Kelley Gordon for the visuals and posters, and Kate Moran and Feifei Liu for updated names, descriptions, and examples. A reuse license for the article text was not on the checked page.
agent_guidance:
Use the ten named principles as a review list when you judge an interface. Read the article for the examples rather than inventing what each heuristic means.

The page is prose. It does not ship components, and it does not grant a license to copy the article text or the poster art.
why_it_matters: It is the canonical short list of interaction-design heuristics, with the original date and a 2024 review still on the page.
tier_reason: A primary source, free to read, with a named author, a 1994 date, and a 2024 review. The article's reuse terms were not stated.
evidence: Checked https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/ on 2026-10-25. The page title, summary, byline, dates, and the ten principle names were in the HTML. A later request the same day returned HTTP 403, so this record uses the first HTTP 200 fetch. Source tweet: https://x.com/nurijanian/status/2113600826874950119.

name: GOV.UK Design System
tagline: UK government styles, components, and patterns, with MIT code in govuk-frontend
description:
The GOV.UK Design System is the published guidance for building UK government services. The homepage says to design a service using GOV.UK styles, components, and patterns. The footer says all content is available under the Open Government Licence v3.0, except where otherwise stated, and marks Crown copyright.

The styles section covers page structure, layout, spacing, typography, colour, and images. The components list on the homepage includes accordion, button, checkboxes, date input, error summary, file upload, radios, select, table, tabs, task list, and text input, among others. The code package is govuk-frontend. npm version 5.14.0 and the GitHub repository both report the MIT license. Open Government Licence is not a facet slug, so the license facet records the code only.
agent_guidance:
Read the design-system page for the component or pattern you need, then install govuk-frontend when you are building a UK government service. The written guidance is Open Government Licence v3.0. The npm package govuk-frontend 5.14.0 is MIT.

The checked pages do not say the package is a React library. Confirm the current install steps in the design system before you add it to a framework project.
why_it_matters: It is the official component and pattern source for UK government services, with a public license on both the writing and the code.
tier_reason: Official, maintained, and licensed. Open Government Licence covers the writing, and govuk-frontend 5.14.0 is MIT.
evidence: Checked https://design-system.service.gov.uk/ on 2026-10-25. The footer states the Open Government Licence v3.0 and Crown copyright. npm registry govuk-frontend 5.14.0 reports MIT. GitHub API for alphagov/govuk-frontend on 2026-10-25 reported MIT, 1,475 stars, and a push on 2026-10-23. Source tweet: https://x.com/nurijanian/status/2113600826874950119.

name: hairline
tagline: 33 isometric SVG figures that follow the pointer, for React and plain DOM
description:
hairline is a set of isometric line figures by Lucas Marques. The homepage says there are thirty-three figures, drawn as SVG with no dependencies, for React or plain DOM. The published version on the page and on npm is 0.5.1. Install is npm i @lucasmarkes/hairline. The site also shows an shadcn registry URL and an llms.txt file.

The homepage and the GitHub LICENSE file both say MIT. The llms.txt file lists one function and one React component per figure, and names all thirty-three: Riffle, Terrain, Exploded, Phosphor, Slow, Turntable, Keyboard, Elevator, Phone, Laptop, Terminal, Cabinet, Branches, Vault, Lockers, Padlock, Patch, Dish, Router, Loupe, Sieve, Rail, Plug, Query, Drawer, Basket, Plot, Hub, Relay, Settle, Format, Rebuild, and Stack.
agent_guidance:
Read https://hairline.lucasmarkes.com/llms.txt before you pick a figure. Install @lucasmarkes/hairline, or add the registry file with npx shadcn@latest add https://hairline.lucasmarkes.com/r/hairline.json.

The package is MIT and has no runtime dependencies. Use a figure as a small illustration, not as a general icon system.
why_it_matters: It gives pointer-reactive isometric drawings as an MIT package, with a text file an agent can read.
tier_reason: MIT, versioned on npm, documented in llms.txt, and updated on GitHub in October 2026.
notable_for: llms.txt and an shadcn registry URL
evidence: Checked https://hairline.lucasmarkes.com/ and https://hairline.lucasmarkes.com/llms.txt on 2026-10-25. npm @lucasmarkes/hairline 0.5.1 reports MIT. The GitHub LICENSE file is the MIT license, copyright 2026 Lucas Marques. GitHub API for lucasmarkes/hairline reported 2,923 stars and a push on 2026-10-14. https://hairline.lucasmarkes.com/r/hairline.json returned HTTP 200 and a shadcn registry item. name: Pele
tagline: Open-source library that renders Mermaid diagrams to SVG themed with CSS variables
description:
Pele renders Mermaid diagram syntax to SVG. The homepage says it is a lightweight open-source library, themed with CSS variables, so color changes apply without a re-render. The documented install is npm install pele, and the example imports render from pele. Docs pages linked from the site cover the API, theming, compatibility, security, and examples.

The homepage claims zero direct dependencies, support for every diagram type built into Mermaid 12.1.0, a 230 kB gzip bundle against 1.6 MB for Mermaid.js, and faster render times. Those performance figures are the site's own comparison, not a measurement made for this record. npm pele 1.10.0 and the GitHub LICENSE file are MIT, copyright 2026 kepano. GitHub's license API returned NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file text is the MIT license.
agent_guidance:
Install pele and pass Mermaid syntax to render(). Insert the returned SVG yourself. Theme it with the --pele-* CSS variables on the homepage rather than re-rendering for a color change.

Read https://pele.run/security before you render untrusted diagram text. The homepage claims Mermaid 12.1.0 coverage. Check the compatibility page when a diagram uses a newer syntax.
why_it_matters: It turns Mermaid text into themed SVG without shipping the Mermaid.js bundle.
tier_reason: MIT on npm and in the LICENSE file, with API docs and a October 2026 commit. The speed and size numbers are the project's own claims.
evidence: Checked https://pele.run/ on 2026-10-25. npm pele 1.10.0 reports MIT. The raw LICENSE file at obsidianmd/pele is the MIT license, copyright 2026 kepano. GitHub API reported 3,497 stars and a push on 2026-10-24. https://pele.run/llms.txt returned 404. Source tweet: https://x.com/noahelhadedy/status/2111868210244948169.

name: Squints
tagline: Free Chrome extension that measures spacing, type, colour, grids, and animation on a live page
description:
Squints is a free Chrome extension for inspecting a live web page. The homepage says it measures a box and the gap to the next one, offers rulers and guides, a column grid remembered per site, drawing tools, a color picker with the token behind the color, font identification with metrics, and controls to slow an animation or scrub it frame by frame.

The page says it is used by 2,000+ designers and engineers and names the maker as Andreas Katzmann, a product designer and frontend engineer near Copenhagen. It says the extension is free. A software license was not stated. A privacy link is on the page. The privacy policy was not opened.
agent_guidance:
Send a person to Squints when they need to measure a live page the way they would measure a Figma frame. It is a Chrome extension, not a library you install in the repo.

The homepage says it is free and claims 2,000+ users. It does not publish a license for the extension code. Do not plan an agent workflow around it.
why_it_matters: It puts Figma-style measuring, type, color, grid, and animation inspection on the shipped page.
tier_reason: The feature list and the free price are on the homepage. License, source, and a changelog were not.
evidence: Checked https://squints.app/ on 2026-10-25. The homepage states the feature list, the free price, the 2,000+ user claim, and the maker credit. A license file was not found on that page. Source tweet: https://x.com/noahelhadedy/status/2111868210244948169.

name: The Iconography Encyclopedia

name: mdxcn
tagline: shadcn-style React components that turn Markdown into docs figures
description:
mdxcn is a set of React components for MDX docs. The homepage says they draw callouts, steps, terminals, timelines, tables, and charts with text, so the same figure can be a React component in MDX or a plain-text block in a README. The site says mdxcn is part of Shadcn Labs and that the license is MIT.

The installation page says there is no npm package. The shadcn CLI copies each component's source into the project and adds motion as the dependency. Commands on that page include npx shadcn@latest add @mdxcn/graph-table and npx shadcn@latest add @mdxcn/all. The homepage says each component has a screen-reader summary. llms.txt is published at https://www.mdxcn.dev/llms.txt. The GitHub LICENSE file is MIT, copyright 2026 Keshav Bagaade.
agent_guidance:
Read https://www.mdxcn.dev/llms.txt first. Add one figure with npx shadcn@latest add @mdxcn/graph-table, or the set with npx shadcn@latest add @mdxcn/all. Register the component in MDX, then write Markdown inside the tag.

There is no npm package to install. In a README or a pull request, paste the plain-text figure from the docs instead of JSX. The homepage says each component has a screen-reader summary.
why_it_matters: It gives docs a text figure that stays readable as Markdown and installs like a shadcn component.
tier_reason: MIT, a public registry command, llms.txt, and a commit the day before this check. Accessibility is claimed, not independently tested.
evidence: Checked https://www.mdxcn.dev/, https://www.mdxcn.dev/llms.txt, and https://www.mdxcn.dev/docs/installation on 2026-10-25. The installation page states there is no npm package and shows the shadcn commands. The GitHub LICENSE file for shadcn-labs/mdxcn is MIT. GitHub API reported 455 stars and a push on 2026-10-24. Source tweet: https://x.com/noahelhadedy/status/2111868210244948169.

name: Mockup Freak
tagline: Browser device and poster mockups in 4K, with free scenes and paid scenes from $2
description:
Mockup Freak is a browser mockup studio for phones, laptops, tablets, and posters. The homepage says you upload a PNG, JPG, or WebP, preview it in the browser, and download a JPG. It says there is no Photoshop step. The homepage says the library has 40 scenes, that 7 scenes are free with a watermark-free JPG and no account, and that individual paid scenes start at $2. Named collections on the page, Wellness, Workspace, Travel, and Nature, are listed at $10.

The pricing page says unlimited access is $39 a month, or $29 a month billed as $87 every 3 months. It also says every mockup is $2, one time, with 4K download and commercial use, and no attribution. A $5 figure appears beside the $2 price. The page does not explain that $5. Paid scenes include a commercial license. Free scenes need no account.
pricing_detail: Free: 7 scenes, watermark-free JPG, no account. Paid scenes from $2, and the pricing page says every mockup is $2 one time with commercial use and no attribution. A $5 figure also appears beside that price and is not explained. Unlimited: $39/month, or $29/month billed $87 every 3 months. Collections listed at $10.
agent_guidance:
Start with the 7 free scenes if you only need a watermark-free JPG and no commercial paperwork. For a paid scene, the pricing page says $2 buys that mockup in 4K with a commercial license and no attribution.

Unlimited use is a subscription: $39 a month, or $29 a month billed quarterly at $87. A $5 figure sits next to the $2 price and is not explained on the page. Read that line again before you quote a per-mockup price.
why_it_matters: It sells specific 4K scenes in the browser, with a free set that does not ask for an account.
tier_reason: Prices and the commercial-use line are published. An unexplained $5 figure sits next to the $2 price.
evidence: Checked https://mockupfreak.com/ and https://mockupfreak.com/pricing on 2026-10-25. The homepage states 40 scenes, 7 free scenes, scene prices from $2, and collections at $10.
